$comment: THE EDGE TRUST POLICY. One registry, two enforcers, one guard.
This file defines the only path by which an application API request may reach a backend, and
the controls that make that path provable rather than merely intended:
client -> Front Door + WAF -> APIM -> backend
APIM is the identity/trust boundary. It is the only place a token is validated and the only
place the closed X-Idp-* contract comes into existence. Backends consume that contract and
never re-derive it.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. Until it did, the model rested on reachability alone: the backends could
not distinguish an APIM-stamped X-Idp-Tenant-Id from one a caller typed, and said so in their
own comments. The constitution is explicit that the network control is NOT sufficient alone
(spec 10.3, 'Neither control is sufficient alone'). A second, application-level control is
therefore required at every leg, and it is defined here so that both stacks enforce the same
one rather than two that drift.

chain.statement: Every application API request traverses Front Door + WAF, then APIM, then the backend. There is no other path, including for service-to-service and Workload calls (spec 13.4).

hops.networkControl: Front Door is the only public DNS name and the only public IP. Backends have no public ingress.
hops.applicationControl: WAF managed rule sets and rate limiting. TLS 1.2 minimum, HTTPS-only.
hops.$comment: Boundary 1 in spec 10.2. Nothing is trusted here; all input is hostile until validated.

hops.networkControl: APIM accepts origin traffic only from the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag; every other source is denied by NSG and by APIM's own network configuration.
hops.applicationControl: APIM rejects any request whose X-Azure-FDID does not equal this platform's Front Door identifier.
$comment: The service tag alone is insufficient: it admits EVERY Azure customer's Front Door,
so an attacker provisions their own profile and points it at this origin. The FDID
check is what makes the origin specific to this platform. Neither control is
sufficient alone (spec 10.3) - this is the pair that sentence names.

hops.networkControl: Container Apps ingress is internal on every application container app; external ingress is prohibited. The backend has no public FQDN and is reachable only from inside the environment's VNet, into which APIM is injected.
hops.applicationControl: APIM presents a client certificate. Ingress validates it and republishes it as X-Forwarded-Client-Cert. The backend refuses any audience request whose forwarded certificate hash is not in the configured allow-list.
$comment: A CERTIFICATE, NOT A SHARED SECRET. A shared secret in a header is a bearer token: it
appears in configuration, in any log that captures headers, and in the memory of every
replica that holds it, and it is replayable by anyone who sees it once. The certificate
is held by APIM, the backend holds only a hash of it, and rotation is an overlap in the
allow-list rather than a synchronised secret swap.
VNet injection alone is insufficient for the same reason the service tag was: it admits
anything already inside the VNet - a compromised sidecar, a misconfigured job, a second
container app - and each of those could then mint any tenant and any role it liked.

identityContract.statement: The closed Gateway-derived header contract (spec 11.5). APIM deletes any inbound copy before validation and sets these on the outbound request. Backends consume them and MUST NOT parse a token.
$comment: CLOSED means five, exactly. A sixth header carrying authority is a second identity
derivation wearing a different name, and the enforcers assert the list length so that
adding one requires editing this file rather than editing one service.

audiences.roles: non-empty subset of administrator, senior_technician, technician

$comment: THE ONLY PATHS THAT MAY BE SERVED WITHOUT PROVENANCE, and the reason each one must be.
Health probes originate from the Container Apps infrastructure itself, not from APIM. They
cannot carry a gateway certificate and there is nothing they could carry instead. They are
also the only anonymous surface (spec 13.6) and they carry no identity, so a request that
reaches one has gained nothing.
This is a prefix list rather than an allow-list of exact paths for a reason the boundary
guard depends on: an allow-list grows an entry at a time, and the entry somebody adds
without thinking is the one that matters. A prefix cannot be extended without moving a
route under /health, which is visible in review.

neverParseTokens.statement: No backend validates, decodes or inspects a bearer token. There is no JWT library on the audience path and no signing key to rotate at this tier.

neverTrustClientAssertedAuthority.statement: Tenant, role, audience, principal and impersonation targets are never accepted from a client field, in any position - header, query parameter, path segment or body.
$comment: Compared with case folded and separators stripped, so tenant_id, tenantId, X-Tenant-Id
and TENANT-ID are one entry rather than four somebody has to remember.
ONE EXCEPTION, and it is a narrowing: tenantId as a read filter on the staff audience.
It selects within the set the caller may already see and confers nothing; the tenant
query filter still applies underneath it, so a value outside that set returns no rows.

rejectSpoofedIdentity.statement: An X-Idp-* header on a request that cannot prove gateway provenance is refused. The request is rejected, not sanitised: stripping the header and continuing would serve an attacker a 200 and leave the attempt indistinguishable from an ordinary call in the logs.

noExternalIngress.statement: No application container app declares external ingress. This is the network half of the apim-to-backend hop and is asserted against the committed manifests.

noDirectServiceToService.statement: A service MUST NOT call another platform service by its internal address (spec 13.4). Cross-service application calls go out through the approved egress path and back in through Front Door and APIM.

$comment: THE VAULT HOLDS THE PRIVATE KEY, APIM HOLDS A REFERENCE, THE BACKENDS HOLD A PUBLIC HASH.
No component in this arrangement holds a standing secret, which is what keeps a client
certificate consistent with build/policy/azure-identity.json rather than an exception to
it. The exemption entry in that file records the residual: the certificate has a lifecycle
and an expiry, which a managed identity would not.
REFERENCED BY certificate-id, NEVER BY THUMBPRINT. A Key Vault certificate's thumbprint
changes on rotation, and an APIM policy identifying it by thumbprint silently fails to
resolve the new certificate - it stops attaching a client certificate at all. That failure
has no error at the gateway; it surfaces only as every backend call losing provenance at
once. check-edge-path.sh asserts the policy does not use the thumbprint attribute.
AUTOMATIC ROTATION IS DELIBERATELY TURNED OFF, by pinning a version in the Key Vault
certificate identifier. This is the one place where the safer-looking Azure default is the
dangerous option, so the reasoning is recorded rather than assumed.
APIM syncs a Key Vault certificate within four hours of it changing. The backends pin the
LEAF hash. So an ordinary certificate renewal in the vault would propagate to APIM on its
own schedule and then every request would begin failing provenance - a total outage, with
no deployment, no code change and no alert that names the cause, triggered by a
certificate doing exactly what it was configured to do.
Nothing in Azure sequences the vault update against the backend allow-list. Until the
deployment pipeline does that sequencing itself, the correct answer is to make rotation a
reviewed release rather than a background job that can take production down unattended.
THE ORDER IS THE CONTROL, and it is widen-then-switch:
1. Add the incoming hash to the allow-list on BOTH deployables. Both are now accepted.
2. Point the APIM certificate entity at the new Key Vault version.
3. Confirm traffic is flowing on the new certificate.
4. Remove the outgoing hash.
There is no instant in that sequence at which neither certificate is accepted. Performing
step 2 before step 1 is a full outage, which is why the runbook leads with the ordering
rather than ending with it.

channels.mechanism: Key Vault certificate lifetime action, EmailContacts
Event Grid CertificateNearExpiry to an Azure Monitor alert
Event Grid CertificateExpired to an Azure Monitor alert

$comment: EXPIRY IS THE RESIDUAL RISK OF THIS WHOLE DESIGN, and pinning the version is what makes it
a real one: nothing renews the certificate on our behalf any more.
An expired gateway certificate is a total, simultaneous outage of every audience on both
deployables, and it arrives on a date that was knowable for a year. Worse, it is a
misleading outage: health probes are exempt from gateway provenance, so every replica stays
green and in rotation while serving nothing, with no deployment in the window to blame. The
alerting is therefore not operational hygiene - it is the control that makes the
pinned-version strategy safe to choose, and the two are adopted together or not at all.
WHY TWO LEAD TIMES RATHER THAN THE ONE WE WANTED. Azure fixes the certificate near-expiry
event at 30 days and exposes no setting for it; only the KEY near-expiry event is
configurable, via the key rotation policy. So the earliest we can be TOLD is 45 days, by
the Key Vault lifetime action, and that channel is email. The earliest we can be WOKEN is
30 days.
Both numbers are recorded because treating the 45 as the deadline would be a mistake: it is
the weaker mechanism, and an unread mailbox during a holiday period consumes the whole
difference. THE 30-DAY PAGE IS THE REAL DEADLINE. The 45-day mail is an advance courtesy
that buys scheduling room, and it is first only because the stronger signal cannot be
moved earlier.
REQUIRED CONFIGURATION, WITH NO DEFAULT AND NO ENVIRONMENT BRANCH. An empty allow-list
fails the process at startup rather than starting one that accepts anything.
This is deliberately harsher than the Key Vault setting next door, which is legitimately
absent on a developer machine. The difference is the failure mode: an unconfigured vault
fails loudly on the first secret it needs, whereas an unconfigured allow-list would fail
silently, by accepting forged identity, and would look exactly like a working service.
There is consequently no local bypass - which matches how identity is already treated. A
developer running either backend directly already has to supply the five X-Idp-* headers
by hand, because the gateway that would normally set them is not there. Supplying a
development certificate hash alongside them is the same exercise, and it means the code
path exercised locally is the code path that runs in production.
The thumbprint is not secret material. It is the hash of a public certificate, so it is
ordinary configuration rather than a Key Vault reference - and treating it as a secret
would wrongly suggest that knowing it is worth anything.
